## Abstract

The Ankobra River Basin has a long history of gold mining activities and the recent intensification of Galamsey (illegal small-scale gold mining) activities has worsened the quality of water resources, especially in the upper part, which was less prone to water quality issues in the past. This study, therefore, is a preliminary assessment of the current spatial and seasonal variations of the water quality, the heavy metal pollution index (HPI), and the factors controlling the sources of variation in the water chemistry in the upper part of the Ankobra Basin impacted by illegal mining activities. Sampling was carried out in December 2017, for the dry season, and August 2018, for the wet season. The groundwater (GW) range of measured values for all parameters passed the 2011 WHO guideline for drinking water permissible limits except for pH, TDS, Fe, Mn, As, and Al, which failed for a sample or a particular season. Likewise, for surface water (SW), the range of measured values for all parameters fell within the WHO acceptable guideline limit except for pH, turbidity, TSS, Fe, Mn, Hg, Cd, Cr, As, and Al in at least a sample or during a particular season. The GW was generally more acidic than the SW. The surface water turbidity ranged from 20 to 29,550 NTU and 22 to 29,550 NTU for the dry and wet seasons. The turbidity was relatively higher in the downstream communities. The SW is unacceptable as a drinking water source as its HPI value (124.78) is above the permissible critical value of 100. The processes contributing to the variation in the surface and groundwater hydrochemistry include the natural evolution of minerals of the geological complex from silicates, carbonates, and sulphides; leaching of trace metals from mine tailings; the oxidation of pyrite; and geogenic contamination caused by elevated Fe and Mn. The release of trace metals, particularly arsenic, and the turbidity of SW have increased due to Galamsey activities even though the general hydrochemistry of the surface–groundwater has not altered.

## Abstract

Artisanal small-scale mining has been part of Ghana’s history, but recent public outcry on the devastating impacts of the phenomenon on water bodies, due to expansion in the sector, has led to clamp downs by various governments on the activity. This has called for evaluation of the water quality of the South-western Rivers System, which are small-scale mining endemic areas. Thirty-five river samples were collected in July 2018 and were analyzed for physico-chemical parameters using procedures outlined in the Standard Methods for the Examination of Water and Wastewaters. The results revealed that the rivers are polluted with Fe and Cu, accompanied by very high levels of turbidity (mean = 488 NTU) and total suspended solids (TSS) (mean = 382 mg/L). NH 3–N, PO 4–P, BOD, and DO levels indicated mild pollution in the waters. Pollution of the rivers is attributable to impacts of artisanal small-scale mining, surface run-off as a result of high intensity rainfall, anthropogenic (indiscriminate waste disposal) and geogenic factors such as dissolution of minerals from the soil zone. It was observed that, if not strictly regulated, turbidity and TSS levels arising mainly from illegal small-scale mining activities could lead to shutdowns of a number of Ghana Water Company Limited treatment plants, leading to water supply challenges in the study area.

## Abstract

Artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) have rendered freshwater resources across the globe unsafe for consumption, posing health risks. The study assessed 15 water quality parameters using standardised water examination protocols. Twenty-four water samples were analysed from the upstream, midstream, and downstream of the Oda River, and the results were compared with the Ghana Standards Authority (GSA) and the World Health Organisation (WHO) water quality benchmarks. The concentrations of electrical conductivity (EC), total dissolved solids (TDS), pH, lead (Pb), cadmium (Cd), mercury (Hg), arsenic (As), fluoride (F), copper (Cu), and cyanide (CN) were within permissible limits. However, the turbidity concentrations are 694, 1755, and 1658 NTU (> 5.0), the total suspended solids (TSS) concentrations are 438, 1380, and 1360 mg/L (> 0), iron (Fe) concentrations are 9.0, 34.0, and 20.0 mg/L (> 0.3 mg/L), faecal coliform concentrations are 180, 145, and 180 MPN/100 mL, and _Escherichia coli_ (_E. coli_) concentrations are 83, 125, and 235 MPN/100 mL (> 0 MPN/100 mL) exceeding the recommended standards. The Principal Component Analysis (CPA) and Hierarchical Cluster Analysis (HCA) suggest low ASM impact in the upstream compared to the midstream and downstream. The Comprehensive Pollution Index (CPI) values of 172.62 in the upstream, 468.68 in the midstream, and 401.31 in the downstream (> 2.0) indicate severe pollution of the Oda River. The study provides invaluable information on the effects of ASM activities on freshwater quality, ecosystems, and public health. The study concludes that ASM activities in freshwater basins obstruct SDG-6 attainment in Ghana and should be banned or properly regulated.

## 1 Introduction

ASM activities pose a substantial threat to water quality on a worldwide scale. Annually, ASM releases 640 to 1350 mg of Hg into the environment in over 70 countries [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR1 "Telmer KH, Veiga MM. World emissions of mercury from artisanal and small scale gold mining BT - Mercury Fate and Transport in the Global Atmosphere: Emissions, Measurements and Models. In: Mason R, Pirrone N, editors., Boston, MA: Springer US; 2009, p. 131–72. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-93958-2_6
                  
                .")]. In regions such as Ghana, the detrimental impacts of potentially toxic elements (PTEs) arising from these operations have rendered water unsuitable for consumption and everyday use [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR2 "Boateng A. Effect of small-scale mining on the environment in Ghana Bachelors Dissertation. Metropolia Univ Appl Sci. 2018;10:12."), [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR3 "Duncan AE, de Vries N, Nyarko KB. Assessment of Heavy metal pollution in the sediments of the river pra and its tributaries. Water Air Soil Pollut. 2018;229:1–10. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/S11270-018-3899-6/TABLES/3
                  
                .")]. This issue directly affects the achievement of Sustainable Development Goal 6 (SDG 6), which aims to ensure the availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR4 "United Nations. The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development’s 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). New York, USA: 2015.")]. Access to clean, potable water is a fundamental human entitlement [[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR5 "World Health Organization. Guidelines for Drinking-Water Quality Fourth Edition WHO Library Cataloguing-in-Publication Data Guidelines for drinking-water quality-4 th edition. Switzerland: WHO Graphics; 2011.")]. However, globally, more than 884 million individuals lack access to clean water due to varying degrees of pollution [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR1 "Telmer KH, Veiga MM. World emissions of mercury from artisanal and small scale gold mining BT - Mercury Fate and Transport in the Global Atmosphere: Emissions, Measurements and Models. In: Mason R, Pirrone N, editors., Boston, MA: Springer US; 2009, p. 131–72. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-93958-2_6
                  
                .")]. This pollution leads to the tragic demise of 1.5 million children under the age of five annually due to water-borne ailments [[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR6 "Aliyu HS, Amanabo M, Musa DA. Assessment of heavy metal pollution of drinking water sources and staple food cultivars around artisanal mining site in Igade-Mashegu, Niger State, Nigeria. World J Biol Pharm Health Sci. 2023;14:306–19. 
                  https://doi.org/10.0574/wjbphs.2023.14.2.0162
                  
                ."), [7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR7 "World Health Organization. Drinking-Water Factsheet. World Health Organization .2023. 
                  https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/drinking-water
                  
                . Accessed 26 May 2024.")]. In Ghana, 671,167 people lack clean water, resulting in waterborne diseases such as diarrhoea, cholera, and typhoid fever [[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR8 "Ghana Statistical Service. Ghana 2021 Population and Housing Census - General Report Volume 3M - Water and Sanitation. Accra, Ghana: 2022.")]. The WHO reports that contaminated drinking water causes 485,000 fatalities from diarrhoeal illnesses annually. Also, approximately 1.7 billion individuals worldwide rely on drinking water contaminated with faecal matter [[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR7 "World Health Organization. Drinking-Water Factsheet. World Health Organization .2023. 
                  https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/drinking-water
                  
                . Accessed 26 May 2024.")]. Waterborne diseases threaten not only SDG 6 but also SDG 3, which targets good health and well-being [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR4 "United Nations. The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development’s 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). New York, USA: 2015.")]. Faecal matter in freshwater bodies in mining communities has been attributed to poor sanitary conditions at ASM sites [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR9 "Goski BNY. The quality of water of the Weija Dam and the Densu River Doctoral Dissertation. Legon: University of Ghana; 1999.")]. This situation underscores the importance of addressing ASM and water pollution to secure access to clean, potable water and align to achieve environmental sustainability under SDG 12, which focuses on responsible consumption and production patterns [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR4 "United Nations. The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development’s 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). New York, USA: 2015.")].

ASM, water contamination, and constrained accessibility to potable water are important worldwide issues, particularly in Africa and the sub-Saharan African region. According to a study by Dietler et al. [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR10 "Dietler D, Farnham A, Loss G, Fink G, Winkler MS.                 .")], unregulated cobalt mining has polluted water sources with PTEs and affected access to clean drinking water for local communities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. In Nigeria, ASM activities in Zamfara State resulted in lead contamination of water sources and culminated in an outbreak of lead poisoning and the deaths of hundreds of children. In Zimbabwe, unregulated gold mining has led to the pollution of rivers and streams and made it challenging for communities to access safe, potable water [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR10 "Dietler D, Farnham A, Loss G, Fink G, Winkler MS. Global Health. 2021;17:1–16. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1186/S12992-021-00723-2/FIGURES/8
                  
                .")]. The consequences of such contamination hinder efforts to achieve SDG 6 and pose long-term environmental challenges under SDG 15, which promotes the sustainable use and protection of terrestrial ecosystems [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR4 "United Nations. The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development’s 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). New York, USA: 2015.")].

In Ghana, ASM activities have led to the pollution of nearly 60% of the freshwater bodies in the country [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR11 "Yeleliere E, Cobbina SJ, Duwiejuah AB.                 .")]. Consequently, in 2017, many water treatment facilities in Ghana ceased operation, and several water sources became unfit for human consumption [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR11 "Yeleliere E, Cobbina SJ, Duwiejuah AB. ASM practices increased turbidity concentrations in the Pra and Birim Rivers [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR11 "Yeleliere E, Cobbina SJ, Duwiejuah AB. Review of Ghana’s water resources: the quality and management with particular focus on freshwater resources. Appl Water Sci. 2018;8:1–12. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/S13201-018-0736-4/TABLES/2
                  
                .")]. Extensive research conducted by the GWCL has indicated that several well-known rivers in the Western Region of Ghana have suffered severe degradation due to ASM activities. The Daboase, Ankobra, and Pra Watercourses were unfit for human consumption. The Enu Watercourse in the Ashanti Region, vital to the residents of Konongo, has been contaminated by ASM operations, and its water was considered unfit for domestic use [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR12 "Citifmonline.com. Galamsey, pollution destroying water bodies in Ghana - Water Company - Citi 97.3 FM - Relevant Radio. Always. Citifmonline.Com. 2017. 
                  https://citifmonline.com/2017/03/galamsey-pollution-destroying-water-bodies-in-ghana-water-company/
                  
                . Accessed 26 May 2024.")]. Additionally, ASM operations have led to the deterioration of the Black Volta watercourse in the Upper West region [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR12 "Citifmonline.com. Galamsey, pollution destroying water bodies in Ghana - Water Company - Citi 97.3 FM - Relevant Radio. Always. Citifmonline.Com. 2017. 
                  https://citifmonline.com/2017/03/galamsey-pollution-destroying-water-bodies-in-ghana-water-company/
                  
                . Accessed 26 May 2024.")]. Research by Aboka et al.[[14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR14 "Aboka EY, Jerry CS, Dzigbodi DA. Review of environmental and health impacts of mining in Ghana. J Health Pollut. 2018;8:43–52. 
                  https://doi.org/10.5696/2156-9614-8.17.43
                  
                .")] reported that the progress of ASM activities in the Obuasi Municipality has resulted in the pollution of rivers such as Wheaseammo, Pompo, Nyam, Kunka, Jimi, Akapori, and Kwabrafo, leading to a shortage of potable water resources and waterborne diseases such as diarrhoea, typhoid, and cholera [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR12 "Citifmonline.com. Galamsey, pollution destroying water bodies in Ghana - Water Company - Citi 97.3 FM - Relevant Radio. Always. Citifmonline.Com. 2017. 
                  https://citifmonline.com/2017/03/galamsey-pollution-destroying-water-bodies-in-ghana-water-company/
                  
                . Accessed 26 May 2024.")].

The Amansie Central District has been facing substantial challenges triggered by ASM endeavours. The Oda River, a crucial source of water for household and agricultural activities in the region, has been affected by illegal mining [[15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR15 "Obeng S. Effects of Illegal Small-Scale Gold Mining Activities on the Environment: Case Study of Selected Communities in the Amansie West District. Bachelors Dissertation. Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, 2015.")]. Research on the three factors used to determine water quality, such as physico-chemical parameters, PTE concentrations, and biological components, is limited. Previous studies focused exclusively on one of these criteria, disregarding the others. For instance, Asare-Donkor et al. [[16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR16 "Asare-Donkor NK, Adimado AA. Influence of mining-related activities on levels of mercury in water, sediment and fish from the Ankobra and Tano River basins in South Western Ghana. Environ Syst Res. 2016;5:1–11. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1186/S40068-016-0055-4
                  
                .")] investigated PTE concentrations but failed to account for the biological and physico-chemical aspects. Bansah et al. [[17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR17 "Bansah KJ, Dumakor-Dupey NK, Kansake BA, Assan E, Bekui P. Socioeconomic and environmental assessment of informal artisanal and small-scale mining in Ghana. J Clean Prod. 2018;202:465–75. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/J.JCLEPRO.2018.08.150
                  
                .")] examined the physico-chemical parameters and PTE concentrations of the Bonsa River and neglected the biological parameters of the river. Duncan et al. [[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR3 "Duncan AE, de Vries N, Nyarko KB. Assessment of Heavy metal pollution in the sediments of the river pra and its tributaries. Water Air Soil Pollut. 2018;229:1–10. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/S11270-018-3899-6/TABLES/3
                  
                .")] explored PTE concentrations in the Pra Watercourse catchment area without considering biological and physico-chemical components. Research by Attiogbe et al. [[18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR18 "Attiogbe FK, Mohammed AR, Kingslove Q. Assessing the potential health impact of selected heavy metals that pollute Lake Amponsah in Bibiani, Western North region. Ghana Sci Afr. 2020;9:1–11. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/J.SCIAF.2020.E00531
                  
                .")] examined PTE concentrations in Lake Amponsah; physico-chemical and biological factors were not considered. Finally, Hadzi et al. [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR19 "Hadzi GY, Essumang DK, Adjei JK. Distribution and risk assessment of heavy metals in surface water from pristine environments and major mining Areas in Ghana. J Health Pollut. 2015;5:86–99. 
                  https://doi.org/10.5696/2156-9614-5-9.86
                  
                .")] studied PTEs while ignoring their physico-chemical and biological characteristics. Therefore, to establish the effect of ASM on the Oda River, it is crucial to examine all three parameter groups used to measure water quality.

Currently, there is limited scientific evidence available about the level of pollution in the Oda River since ASM activities took place in the Oda Basin in the late 2000s. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the freshwater quality in the Oda River by examining its physico-chemical and biological properties and the presence of PTEs. Additionally, the study used a comprehensive water pollution index to determine the suitability of the Oda River for human consumption and the pollution status of the river. The study informs policies, laws, and regulations on ASM activities for freshwater resources and also contributes to SDGs 6, 3, 12, and 15, providing crucial evidence to support strategies aimed at reducing pollution and protecting water resources.

## 2 Methods and materials

### 2.1 Research site and sampling points

The study focused on different sections of the Oda River – upstream region, midstream section, and downstream—within the Amansie Central District (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#Fig1)), a district that recorded a population of 93,052 individuals based on the 2021 census [[20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR20 "Ghana Statistical Service. Multidimensional Poverty Report - Amansie Central District. Accra: Ghana: 2024.")]. The Oda River, with a basin covering an area of 168.21 km 2 [[21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR21 "ProtectedPlanet.net. Explore the World’s Protected Areas: Oda River. ProtectedPlanet.Net. 2020. 
                  https://www.protectedplanet.net/40685
                  
                . Accessed 26 May 2024.")], was selected for this research due to the ongoing ASM challenges. Despite attempts at regulation and an anti-galamsey task force establishment, ASM operations continue to intensify significantly [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR22 "Donkor P, Siabi EK, Frimpong K, Mensah SK, Siabi ES, Vuu C. Socio-demographic effects on role assignment and associated occupational health and safety issues in artisanal and small-scale gold mining in Amansie Central District. Ghana Heliyon. 2023;9: e13741. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heliyon.2023.e13741
                  
                .")]. Consequently, these mining activities have severely affected water quality, especially regarding the use of the river for drinking and household purposes.

### 2.2 Water sampling and distribution

This research assessed fifteen key water quality parameters, including turbidity, TSS, EC, TDS, pH, Cu, Fe, Pb, Hg, Cd, As, F, CN, _E. coli,_ and faecal coliform bacteria, and compared the results with GSA and WHO drinking water standards. Eight water samples each were gathered from the upstream, midstream, and downstream areas of the Oda River, each placed in 500-mL containers (Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#Tab1)). These containers were thoroughly cleaned by rinsing three times, sealed securely, and marked. The samples were labelled upstream 1 and 2, midstream 1 and 2, and downstream 1 and 2 for identification. The collected samples were transported in an ice chest containing ice packs to preserve their condition and sent to the water laboratory in Accra for further investigation. Of the 24 samples collected, six were directed to the microbiology laboratory of GSA to evaluate _E. coli_ and faecal coliform bacteria. Another six samples were delivered to the Envaserv Research Consult to assess fluoride concentrations. Additionally, six samples underwent analysis in the metal laboratory at GSA for elements such as Hg, Cd, Fe, Pb, Cu, As, and CN. The final six samples were used in the water laboratory at GSA to measure EC, turbidity, pH, TDS, and TSS (Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#Tab1)).

### 2.3 Data analysis

Throughout the field and laboratory phases of this study, adherence to established protocols from the Standard Methods for Water Examination, as outlined by the American Public Health Association [[23](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR23 "Association APH. Standard Methods for the examination of water and wastewater, 23rd edition. 23rd ed. Washington: American Public Health Association, American Water Works Association, Water Environment Federation; 2017.")], was followed. The pH values were determined using Ghana Standards (GS ISO 10523) derived from the International Organisation for Standardisation (ISO). Turbidity was evaluated in accordance with GS ISO 7027, while TSS were analysed using the photometric method 8006. For TDS, the gravimetric method was employed. EC measurements followed the ISO 7888 standard. The Pb, Cd, As, Cu, and Fe concentrations were analysed using ISO 8288, while Hg concentrations were assessed with ISO 8088. CN concentrations were measured using the pyridine-pyrazalone method 8027. The fluoride concentration was determined using the Palin test Phot 14 method. For biological parameters such as _E. coli_ and faecal coliform bacteria, the ISO 9308–2 1990–10 method was used. Quality control and assurance measures included calibrating the instrument before each test, and all procedures were conducted three times with the average result recorded.

The mean values for the water parameters and the CPI calculations for the sampling locations were computed with Microsoft Excel 2016. R programming was employed in the PCA and HCA analyses. The CPI was calculated using the formula: CPI = (1/n) Σ(Ci/Si). Where: Ci represents the measured concentration of the pollutant, Si denotes the national standard limit for the pollutant, and n is the total number of pollutants considered. The Pollution Index (PI) was calculated for each pollutant as PI = Ci/Si [[24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR24 "Egun NK, Oboh IP. Surface water quality evaluation of Ikpoba reservoir, EDO State, Nigeria. Int J Energy and Water Resour. 2022;6:509–19. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s42108-021-00139-z
                  
                .")]. Nine pollutants were considered for the calculations of the CPI because they had measured concentration values and national standard limit values. The interpretation of CPI values is as follows: 0–0.2 indicates clean conditions, 0.21–0.4 suggests sub-clean conditions, 0.41–1.0 represents slightly polluted conditions, 1.01–2.0 indicates moderately polluted conditions, and > 2.0 signifies severely polluted conditions [[24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR24 "Egun NK, Oboh IP. Surface water quality evaluation of Ikpoba reservoir, EDO State, Nigeria. Int J Energy and Water Resour. 2022;6:509–19. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s42108-021-00139-z
                  
                .")].

## 3 Results and discussions

### 3.1 Concentration of water quality parameters

The pH values of the Oda River samples ranged from 6.75 to 7.30 across the upstream, midstream, and downstream sampling points (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#Tab2)). These values fall within the acceptable range of 6.5–8.5 recommended by the GSA and WHO for freshwater resources [[25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR25 "Ghana Standards Authority. GS 175: Water Quality- Specification for Drinking Water. Accra: Ghana: 2017."), [26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR26 "World Health Organization. Fourth edition incorporating the first and second addenda Guidelines for drinking-water quality. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2022.")]. The observed pH values suggest that ASM activities have not significantly altered the acidity or alkalinity of the Oda River water. However, these findings contrast studies on other rivers impacted by ASM in Ghana. For instance, Gyekye et al. [[27](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR27 "Gyekye KA, Owusu P, Ofori A. Gold mining effects on water quality in Domenase and Nkotumso along River Offin, Upper Denkyira West District. West Afr J Appl Ecol. 2023;31:10.")] reported pH values between 5.24 and 5.83 in Domenase, a gold mine area along the Offin River in the Upper Denkyira West District. Our findings are also consistent with the study by Aikins et al. [[28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR28 "Aikins S, Gyawu-Asante FN, Voegborlo RB. Physico-chemical quality of water in the gold mining areas of Bibiani, Ghana. Int J Innov Sci Eng Technol. 2015;2:229–38.")], which revealed pH values between 6.57 and 7.14 in surface water in areas with active gold mining in Bibiani.

**Table 2 Water Quality Parameters**

Based on the data, the TDS concentrations in the upstream (91 mg/L), midstream (79 mg/L), and downstream (79 mg/L) sections of the Oda Watercourse are all below the limits established by the GSA (500 mg/L) and the WHO (1000 mg/L). The observed TDS concentrations in the Oda River indicate minimal impact from mining activities, contrasting with the elevated TDS concentrations (up to 6127 mg/L) reported in other mining-affected rivers in Ghana, such as the Subri River in Akem Abuakwa in the Atiwa District [[29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR29 "Attua EM, Annan ST, Nyame F. Water quality analysis of rivers used as drinking sources in artisanal gold mining communities of the Akyem-Abuakwa area: a multivariate statistical approach. Ghana J Geogr. 2014;6:24–41.")]. Our findings are also consistent with the study by Darko et al. [[30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR30 "Darko HF, Karikari AY, Duah AA, Akurugu BA, Mante V, Teye FO. Effect of small-scale illegal mining on surface water and sediment quality in Ghana. Int J River Basin Manage. 2023;21:375–86. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1080/15715124.2021.2002345
                  
                .")], which showed that TDS concentrations in all water sources analysed were below the recommended benchmark value, ranging from 14.0 to 316 mg/L.

The concentrations of TSS in the Oda River are excessively high in the upstream (438 mg/L), midstream (1380 mg/L), and downstream (1360 mg/L). These elevated concentrations are primarily attributed to the intensive ASM activities in the region[[31](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR31 "Hilson G, Maconachie R. Artisanal and small-scale mining and the sustainable development goals: opportunities and new directions for sub-Saharan Africa. Geoforum. 2020;111:125–41. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geoforum.2019.09.006
                  
                .")]. The TSS concentrations of the Oda River exceeded the GSA recommended maximum limit of 0 mg/L for surface water [[25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR25 "Ghana Standards Authority. GS 175: Water Quality- Specification for Drinking Water. Accra: Ghana: 2017.")]. While the WHO guidelines do not specify a standard value for TSS in drinking water, they recommend minimising TSS concentrations through proper treatment and disinfection [[26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR26 "World Health Organization. Fourth edition incorporating the first and second addenda Guidelines for drinking-water quality. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2022.")]. These findings support the findings of Asamoah-Boateng [[32](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR32 "Asamoah-boateng EK. Physico-Chemical and Microbiological Quality of Surface Waters within the Newmont Ghana Gold Mining Concession Areas. Masters dissertation. Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, 2009.")], which discovered the TSS of all the water bodies in the Newmont Ghana Gold Mining Concession Areas ranged from 3.10 to 538.0 mg/L. Our findings also confirm the study by Mambou-Ngueyep et al. [[33](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR33 "Mambou-Ngueyep LL, Takougang Kingni S, Ayiwouo Ngounouno M, Ndi AA. The impact of gold mining exploitation on the physicochemical quality of water: case of Batouri (Cameroon). Int J Energy Water Resourc. 2021;5:159–73. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s42108-020-00106-0
                  
                .")], which discovered high TSS concentrations in rivers in Batouri, Cameroon.

The turbidity concentrations of the Oda River measured upstream (694 NTU), midstream (1755 NTU), and downstream (1658 NTU) all exceeded the safe drinking water recommendation of 5.0 NTU by the GSA and WHO (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#Tab2)). This demonstrates that ASM activities resulted in TSS concentrations in the Oda River exceeding the safety standards for drinking water set by the WHO and GSA. These elevated turbidity concentrations indicate significant water quality degradation due to ASM activities in the region [[31](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR31 "Hilson G, Maconachie R. Artisanal and small-scale mining and the sustainable development goals: opportunities and new directions for sub-Saharan Africa. Geoforum. 2020;111:125–41. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geoforum.2019.09.006
                  
                .")]. The high turbidity values observed in the Oda River can clog fish gills, leading to respiratory distress and potential population declines [[34](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR34 "Kimmel WG, Argent DG. stream fish community responses to a gradient of specific conductance. Water Air Soil Pollut. 2010;206:49–56. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s11270-009-0085-x
                  
                .")]. These findings are consistent with the work of Goski[[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR9 "Goski BNY. The quality of water of the Weija Dam and the Densu River Doctoral Dissertation. Legon: University of Ghana; 1999.")], who observed turbidity concentrations ranging from 6 to 54 NTU in the Densu River Basin. The finding also aligns with Rakotondrabe et al.’s [[35](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR35 "Rakotondrabe F, Ngoupayou JRN, Mfonka Z, Rasolomanana EH, Nyangono Abolo AJ, Asone BL, et al. Assessment of surface water quality of Bétaré-Oya gold mining area (East-Cameroon). J Water Resour Prot. 2017;09:960–84. 
                  https://doi.org/10.4236/jwarp.2017.98064
                  
                .")] research that reported high concentrations of turbidity in the water of the Bétaré-Oya Gold Mining Area in East Cameroon.

The EC of the Oda River varies between 153 µS/cm and 181 µS/cm, with upstream, midstream, and downstream values of 181 µS/cm, 153 µS/cm, and 158 µS/cm, respectively (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#Tab2)). While the drinking water quality guidelines in the GSA [[25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR25 "Ghana Standards Authority. GS 175: Water Quality- Specification for Drinking Water. Accra: Ghana: 2017.")] and the WHO [[26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR26 "World Health Organization. Fourth edition incorporating the first and second addenda Guidelines for drinking-water quality. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2022.")] do not provide a specific EC guideline value, they recommend monitoring EC values. This helps detect changes in water quality and assess treatment processes. These EC values are relatively low compared to other rivers affected by ASM activities in Ghana, suggesting that the Oda River may be less impacted by such operations [[36](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR36 "Kusi-Ampofo S, Boachie-Yiadom T. Assessing the social and environmental impacts of illegal mining operations in River Bonsa Prepared By Pure Fm-Tarkwa, for the BUSAC Project. Tarkwa, Ghana: 2012.")].

The Pb concentrations in the Oda River were within safe limits for drinking water compared to the GSA and WHO water quality guidelines. The upstream (0.01 mg/L), midstream (0.01 mg/L), and downstream (0.004 mg/L) concentrations of Pb were all lower than the maximum permissible limits set by the GSA and WHO guidelines (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#Tab2)). However, it is important to note that even low concentrations of Pb exposure can have adverse health effects, particularly in children and pregnant women [[37](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR37 "Lanphear BP, Rauch S, Auinger P, Allen RW, Hornung RW. Articles Low-level lead exposure and mortality in US adults: a population-based cohort study. Lancet Public Health. 2018;3:e177–84. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/S2468-2667(18)30025-2
                  
                .")]. This observation aligns with a study by Ansa-Asare et al. [[38](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR38 "Ansa-Asare OD, Gordon C. Water quality assessment of Densu, Birim and Ayensu Rivers in the Okyeman Area. West Afr J Appl Ecol. 2012;20:10.")] on the Birim River in Ghana, which found lead concentrations within acceptable limits. However, it contrasts the investigation conducted by Obiri-Yeboah et al. [[39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR39 "Obiri-Yeboah A, Nyantakyi EK, Mohammed AR, Yeboah SIIK, Domfeh MK, Abokyi E. Assessing potential health effect of lead and mercury and the impact of illegal mining activities in the Bonsa river, Tarkwa Nsuaem. Ghana Sci Afr. 2021;13: e00876. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/J.SCIAF.2021.E00876
                  
                .")] on the Bonsu River, which revealed high concentrations of Pb pollution exceeding WHO limits. As a result, the Oda River currently appears safe for human consumption, and children living in the Oda Basin are at lower risk of lead-related diseases compared to areas with higher contamination levels [[40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR40 "Armah FA, Quansah R, Luginaah I. A systematic review of heavy metals of anthropogenic origin in environmental media and biota in the context of gold mining in Ghana. Int Sch Res Notices. 2014;2014:1–37. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1155/2014/252148
                  
                .")].

Cd concentrations within the Oda River were 0.0003 mg/L in the upstream, 0.0004 mg/L in the midstream, and 0.0001 mg/L in the downstream. The Cd concentrations are significantly below the recommended WHO (0.003 mg/L) and the GSA (0.003 mg/L) limits for drinking water (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#Tab2)). The presence of Cd in the Oda River, albeit at low concentrations, can be attributed to ASM activities in the region [[41](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR41 "Hilson G. The environmental impact of small-scale gold mining in Ghana: identifying problems and possible solutions. Geogr J. 2002;168:57–72. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/1475-4959.00038
                  
                .")]. This finding aligns with studies conducted in other ASM-affected areas of Ghana, such as the work by Kpan et al. [[42](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR42 "Kpan JDA, Opoku BK, Gloria A. Heavy metal pollution in soil and water in some selected towns in Dunkwa-on-Offin District in the Central Region of Ghana as a result of small-scale gold mining. J Agric Chem Environ. 2014;03:40–7. 
                  https://doi.org/10.4236/jacen.2014.32006
                  
                .")] in the Tarkwa mining area, where Cd concentrations in water bodies were also below WHO guidelines. However, our finding contradicts Cobbina et al. [[43](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR43 "Cobbina S, Myilla M, Kumi M. Small scale gold mining and heavy metal pollution: assessment of drinking water sources in Datuku in the Talensi-Nabdam District. Int J Sci Technol Res. 2013;2:96–100.")], whose findings reported Cd concentrations between 0.005 and 0.029 mg/L at Datuku within the Talensi-Nabdam District, which exceeded the safety limits set by the WHO drinking water standard.

The concentrations of Hg in the upstream (0.0004 mg/L), midstream (0.001 mg/L), and downstream (0.0003 mg/L) of the Oda Watercourse were below the potable water quality criteria (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#Tab2)). These criteria were promulgated by both the WHO (0.006 mg/L) and the GSA (0.001 mg/L). Chronic exposure to low concentrations of Hg has been associated with subtle neurobehavioral effects and cardiovascular issues [[44](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR44 "Rice KM, Walker EM, Wu M, Gillette C, Blough ER. Environmental mercury and Its toxic effects. J Prev Med Public Health. 2014;47:74–83. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3961/jpmph.2014.47.2.74
                  
                .")]. The presence of Hg in the Oda River is primarily attributed to its use in gold amalgamation processes by ASM miners [[45](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR45 "Aragón FM, Rud JP. Polluting industries and agricultural productivity: evidence from mining in Ghana. Econ J. 2016;126:1980–2011. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/ecoj.12244
                  
                .")]. Our findings align with the study by Francis et al. [[46](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR46 "Francis A, Nkansah A. The impact of mining on the water resources in Ghana: newmont case study at Birim north district (New Abirem). Energy Environ Res. 2017;7:27–36. 
                  https://doi.org/10.5539/eer.v7n2p27
                  
                .")], which reported that the quantity of Hg in the River Pra in Ghana was 0.0002 mg/L. This was also below the drinking water standards set by the GSA and the WHO.

There is an absence of discernible traces of the Cu element in water samples collected from the upstream, midstream, and downstream of the Oda River (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#Tab2)). This shows that gastrointestinal issues such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, and liver and kidney damage associated with drinking Cu-contaminated water are avoided [[47](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR47 "Taylor AA, Tsuji JS, Garry MR, McArdle ME, Goodfellow WL, Adams WJ, et al. Critical review of exposure and effects: implications for setting regulatory health criteria for ingested copper. Environ Manage. 2020;65:131–59. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/S00267-019-01234-Y/TABLES/5
                  
                ."), [48](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR48 "Macdonald KF, Lund MA, Blanchette ML, Mccullough CD. Regulation of artisanal small-scale gold mining (ASGM) in Ghana and Indonesia, as currently implemented, fails to adequately protect aquatic ecosystems. Proceedings of International Mine Water Association Symposium, Xuzhou, China: IMWA; 2014, p. 401–5.")]. This observation contradicts the findings of Francis et al. [[46](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR46 "Francis A, Nkansah A. The impact of mining on the water resources in Ghana: newmont case study at Birim north district (New Abirem). Energy Environ Res. 2017;7:27–36. 
                  https://doi.org/10.5539/eer.v7n2p27
                  
                .")], who discovered traces of Cu in water samples from the Birim River.

The Oda River exhibited elevated Fe concentrations. The concentrations reached in the upstream region (9 mg/L), midstream segment (34 mg/L), and downstream portion (20 mg/L). These concentrations exceeded the recommended drinking requirements delineated by the GSA (0.3 mg/L) and the WHO (0.3 mg/L). The activities of ASM resulted in high Fe concentration in the Oda River. The excessive Fe concentrations in the Oda River can potentially lead to various health issues, including oxidative stress and cellular damage, particularly affecting the liver and heart [[49](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR49 "Jaishankar M, Tseten T, Anbalagan N, Mathew BB, Beeregowda KN. Toxicity, mechanism and health effects of some heavy metals. Interdiscip Toxicol. 2014;7:60–72. 
                  https://doi.org/10.2478/intox-2014-0009
                  
                .")]. These findings align with the investigation by Bawa et al. [[50](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR50 "Bawa SA, Antwi-Agyei P, Domfeh MK. Impact of the ban on illegal mining activities on raw water quality: a case-study of Konongo water treatment plant, Ashanti Region of Ghana. J Sustain Mining. 2022;21:80–92. 
                  https://doi.org/10.46873/2300-3960.1349
                  
                .")], which discovered high Fe concentrations (16.43 to 11.0 mg/L and 314.09 to 11.63 mg/L) within the Fena Watercourse. Rakotondrabe et al.[[35](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR35 "Rakotondrabe F, Ngoupayou JRN, Mfonka Z, Rasolomanana EH, Nyangono Abolo AJ, Asone BL, et al. Assessment of surface water quality of Bétaré-Oya gold mining area (East-Cameroon). J Water Resour Prot. 2017;09:960–84. 
                  https://doi.org/10.4236/jwarp.2017.98064
                  
                .")] also reported elevated Fe concentrations in the surface water of the Bétaré-Oya Gold Mining Area in East Cameroon.

The concentrations of As in the upstream (0.01 mg/L), midstream (0.01 mg/L), and downstream (0.01 mg/L) of the Oda River (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#Tab2)) were within what is recommended for drinking by the WHO (0.01 mg/L) and GSA (0.01 mg/L). However, As concentrations, while acceptable for drinking water standards, may still pose long-term risks if consistently consumed [[51](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR51 "Smith AH, Steinmaus CM. Health effects of arsenic and chromium in drinking water: recent human findings. Annu Rev Public Health. 2009;30:107–22. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.publhealth.031308.100143
                  
                .")]. Even at these low concentrations, As presence in the river indicates the influence of ASM activities in the Oda Basin [[52](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR52 "Obiri S, Yeboah P, Osae S, Adu-Kumi S, Cobbina S, Armah F, et al. Human health risk assessment of artisanal miners exposed to toxic chemicals in water and sediments in the PresteaHuni Valley District of Ghana. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2016;13:139. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph13010139
                  
                .")]. This shows diseases related to (As) water contamination, such as skin, lung, and bladder cancer and cardiovascular lesions, cardiac diseases, and neurological disorders, may not be immediately prevalent but could potentially develop over extended periods of exposure[[53](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR53 "Martinez VD, Vucic EA, Becker-Santos DD, Gil L, Lam WL. Arsenic exposure and the induction of human cancers. J Toxicol. 2011;2011:1–13. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1155/2011/431287
                  
                ."), [54](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR54 "Naujokas MF, Anderson B, Ahsan H, Aposhian HV, Graziano JH, Thompson C, et al. The broad scope of health effects from chronic arsenic exposure: update on a worldwide public health problem. Environ Health Perspect. 2013;121:295–302. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1289/ehp.1205875
                  
                .")]. These findings are consistent with Cobbina et al.’s [[43](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR43 "Cobbina S, Myilla M, Kumi M. Small scale gold mining and heavy metal pollution: assessment of drinking water sources in Datuku in the Talensi-Nabdam District. Int J Sci Technol Res. 2013;2:96–100.")] research at Datuku within the Talensi-Nabdam District, which reported that the concentrations of As were within the safe limits set by the WHO for potable water consumption.

Total cyanide is the combined concentration of free and complex CN in water. Analysis of water samples from various points along the Oda River (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#Tab2)) revealed CN was not detected at any location, including upstream, midstream, and downstream sites. This shows that diseases associated with water contaminated with CN, such as damage to the nervous system, cardiovascular system, thyroid gland, and cancer risk, are avoided in the Oda Basin [[55](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR55 "Yadav P, Verma M, Mishra V. Cyanide: Sources, health issues, and remediation methods. Boca Raton: CRC Press; 2022. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1201/9781003004684-19
                  
                .")]. This finding contradicts the results by Francis et al. [[46](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR46 "Francis A, Nkansah A. The impact of mining on the water resources in Ghana: newmont case study at Birim north district (New Abirem). Energy Environ Res. 2017;7:27–36. 
                  https://doi.org/10.5539/eer.v7n2p27
                  
                .")], who discovered CN traces in water samples from the Birim River.

The F concentrations in the Oda River upstream, midstream, and downstream were less than 0.01 mg/L (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#Tab2)). This is well below the acceptable limits by the GSA and the WHO for drinking water quality (1.5 mg/L for both) [[25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR25 "Ghana Standards Authority. GS 175: Water Quality- Specification for Drinking Water. Accra: Ghana: 2017."), [26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR26 "World Health Organization. Fourth edition incorporating the first and second addenda Guidelines for drinking-water quality. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2022.")]. These low F concentrations in the Oda River suggest the risk of dental fluorosis and skeletal fluorosis from water consumption in the Oda Basin is minimal [[56](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR56 "Fawell J, Bailey K, Chilton J, Dahi E, Fewtrell L, Magara Y. Fluoride in drinking-water. Cornwall, UK: World Health Organization; 2006.")]. These findings regarding F concentrations are consistent with a previous study conducted at the Mpaem Akwa Mines site by Ofosu et al. [[57](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR57 "Ofosu G, Sarpong D. Beyond the doom: sustainable water management practices of small-scale mining operations. Resour Policy. 2022;77:1–8. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/J.RESOURPOL.2022.102649
                  
                .")], which also found F concentrations within acceptable limits.

The study revealed significant faecal coliform contamination in the Oda River, with concentrations of 180 MPN/100 mL upstream, 145 MPN/100 mL midstream, and 180 MPN/100 mL downstream (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#Tab2)). These concentrations substantially exceeded the drinking water quality standards by the GSA and WHO [[25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR25 "Ghana Standards Authority. GS 175: Water Quality- Specification for Drinking Water. Accra: Ghana: 2017."), [26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR26 "World Health Organization. Fourth edition incorporating the first and second addenda Guidelines for drinking-water quality. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2022.")], which mandate a faecal coliform concentration of 0 MPN/100 mL in potable water. The presence of faecal coliform bacteria in the Oda River can be attributed to the prevalence of open defecation and poor sanitary conditions at the ASM sites. The high faecal coliform bacteria concentrations in the Oda River can lead to waterborne illnesses such as choleric infections, typhoid fever, and diarrhoeal episodes. Comparable findings were reported by Goski[[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR9 "Goski BNY. The quality of water of the Weija Dam and the Densu River Doctoral Dissertation. Legon: University of Ghana; 1999.")] in Weija Dam and Densu, where total faecal coliform bacteria fluctuated within 100 to 1940 counts per 100 mL. Our findings also confirm Acheampong et al. [[58](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR58 "Acheampong MA, Paksirajan K, Lens PNL. Assessment of the effluent quality from a gold mining industry in Ghana. Environ Sci Pollut Res. 2013;20:3799–811. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s11356-012-1312-3
                  
                .")] research that reported similar results for total coliforms in the Pra River basin, another gold mining area in Ghana. This indicates that unsatisfactory surroundings prevailed within the respective water basins.

_E. coli_ in freshwater bodies serves as an indicator of faecal impurities and has the potential to cause waterborne illnesses [[59](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR59 "Odonkor ST, Mahami T. Escherichia coli as a tool for disease risk assessment of drinking water sources. Int J Microbiol. 2020;2020:1–7. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1155/2020/2534130
                  
                .")]. The concentrations of the _E. coli_ bacteria in the water samples obtained from the Oda Watercourse exceeded the recommended guidelines for safe drinking water established by the GSA and WHO (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#Tab2)). The Oda River, significantly impacted by ASM activities, shows elevated levels of _E. coli_ contamination [[48](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR48 "Macdonald KF, Lund MA, Blanchette ML, Mccullough CD. Regulation of artisanal small-scale gold mining (ASGM) in Ghana and Indonesia, as currently implemented, fails to adequately protect aquatic ecosystems. Proceedings of International Mine Water Association Symposium, Xuzhou, China: IMWA; 2014, p. 401–5.")]. This contamination is primarily attributed to the lack of proper sanitation facilities at ASM sites, leading to open defecation and direct discharge of untreated waste into the river [[60](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR60 "Bansah KJ, Yalley AB, Dumakor-Dupey N. The hazardous nature of small scale underground mining in Ghana. J Sustain Mining. 2016;15:8–25. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsm.2016.04.004
                  
                .")]. The pathogens can cause health problems such as bloody diarrhoea, low platelet count, renal insufficiency, anaemia, destruction of red blood cells, and complications in the central nervous system. This observation aligns with the revelations documented by Odonkor et al. [[59](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR59 "Odonkor ST, Mahami T. Escherichia coli as a tool for disease risk assessment of drinking water sources. Int J Microbiol. 2020;2020:1–7. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1155/2020/2534130
                  
                .")]. Furthermore, the study conducted by Akabzaa et al. [[61](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR61 "Akabzaa T, Banoeng-Yakubo B, Seyire J. Impact of mining activities on water resources in the vicinity of the Obuasi mine. West Afr J Appl Ecol. 2009;11:1–10. 
                  https://doi.org/10.4314/wajae.v11i1.45719
                  
                .")] in the Tarkwa mining region of Ghana revealed similar patterns of water contamination due to ASM activities, highlighting the widespread nature of this issue in gold-rich areas of the country.

### 3.2 Principal component analysis

Principal Component Analysis is a statistical data-analytic technique for reducing the dimensionality of large datasets and retaining most of the variation in the data.

Figure[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#Fig2) illustrates the results of the PCA conducted on water quality parameters measured at three sampling points along the Oda River: upstream, midstream, and downstream. The PCA effectively reduced the multidimensional dataset to two principal components, with the first dimension (Dim1) explaining an overwhelming 98.5% of the total variance. Dim 1 was primarily driven by EC, pH, turbidity, TSS, and Fe, indicating substantial variance associated with the physico-chemical properties of the samples. In contrast, the second dimension (Dim 2) was characterised by Cd, Pb, _E. coli_, Hg, and faecal coliforms as the key contributors, reflecting minor variances in the PTEs and microbial contamination. This suggests a strong underlying structure in the data, likely dominated by mining-related impacts on water quality [[62](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR62 "Machiwal D, Jha MK. Identifying sources of groundwater contamination in a hard-rock aquifer system using multivariate statistical analyses and GIS-based geostatistical modeling techniques. J Hydrol Reg Stud. 2015;4:80–110. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejrh.2014.11.005
                  
                .")]. The high explanatory power of Dim1 indicates that ASM activities may exert a consistent and significant influence on water quality parameters along the course of the river [[63](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR63 "Asamoah E, Zhang L, Liu G, Owusu-Prempeh N, Rukundo E. Estimating the “Forgone” ESVs for small-scale gold mining using historical image data. Sustainability. 2017;9:1976. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/su9111976
                  
                .")]. Figure[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#Fig2) distinguishes between the three sampling locations, potentially reflecting the varying intensity of ASM activities along the river. The upstream site, positioned in the positive quadrant of Dim1 and Dim2, may represent conditions less impacted by mining.

### 3.3 Hierarchical cluster analysis

The HCA is used to cluster the water quality parameters into respective groups based on their similarities, or distances, from each other.

The hierarchical clustering dendrogram (Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#Fig3)) offers valuable insights into the potential impacts of ASM on the Oda River in the Ashanti Region of Ghana. The dendrogram reveals three distinct clusters: upstream, midstream, and downstream, representing sampling locations along the Oda River. The upstream cluster is markedly separated from midstream and downstream, indicating potentially less impacted water quality conditions as it branches off at the highest point (around height 1000). This aligns with findings by Macdonald et al. [[48](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR48 "Macdonald KF, Lund MA, Blanchette ML, Mccullough CD. Regulation of artisanal small-scale gold mining (ASGM) in Ghana and Indonesia, as currently implemented, fails to adequately protect aquatic ecosystems. Proceedings of International Mine Water Association Symposium, Xuzhou, China: IMWA; 2014, p. 401–5.")], who noted that upstream areas in ASM-affected rivers often serve as reference sites for near-pristine conditions. The closer relationship between midstream and downstream clusters suggests comparable water quality characteristics. This pattern is consistent with the cumulative impacts of ASM activities observed in other Ghanaian rivers [[52](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR52 "Obiri S, Yeboah P, Osae S, Adu-Kumi S, Cobbina S, Armah F, et al. Human health risk assessment of artisanal miners exposed to toxic chemicals in water and sediments in the PresteaHuni Valley District of Ghana. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2016;13:139. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph13010139
                  
                .")]. The dendrogram implies a concentration of mining activities in mid- to downstream areas. This distribution is typical in many ASM-affected watersheds, as showed by Mantey et al. [[65](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR65 "Mantey J, Nyarko KB, Owusu-Nimo F, Awua KA, Bempah CK, Amankwah RK, et al. Mercury contamination of soil and water media from different illegal artisanal small-scale gold mining operations (galamsey). Heliyon. 2020;6: e04312. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heliyon.2020.e04312
                  
                .")] in their study of galamsey operations in Ghana. The midstream and downstream cluster similarity suggests persistent and potentially cumulative effects of ASM on water quality. This observation aligns with the findings of Kusi-Ampofo and Boachie-Yiadom [[36](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR36 "Kusi-Ampofo S, Boachie-Yiadom T. Assessing the social and environmental impacts of illegal mining operations in River Bonsa Prepared By Pure Fm-Tarkwa, for the BUSAC Project. Tarkwa, Ghana: 2012.")] on the Birim River, where ASM impacts intensified downstream. The distinct clustering suggests that management efforts should be tailored to specific river sections. Hilson and Maconachie [[31](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR31 "Hilson G, Maconachie R. Artisanal and small-scale mining and the sustainable development goals: opportunities and new directions for sub-Saharan Africa. Geoforum. 2020;111:125–41. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geoforum.2019.09.006
                  
                .")] emphasise the importance of location-specific strategies in addressing ASM impacts on water resources. The stark difference between upstream and other areas suggests that ASM impacts may be reversible if managed properly. This observation supports the findings of Gyamfi et al. [[66](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR66 "Gyamfi E, Appiah-Adjei EK, Adjei KA. Potential heavy metal pollution of soil and water resources from artisanal mining in Kokoteasua. Ghana Groundw Sustain Dev. 2019;8:450–6. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gsd.2019.01.007
                  
                .")] on the recovery potential of ASM-impacted rivers in Ghana when appropriate interventions are implemented.

### 3.4 Comprehensive water pollution index

The Comprehensive Water Pollution Index is developed using the Single Factor Pollution Index method.

The CPI calculations (Table[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#Tab3)) for the Oda River in the Ashanti Region of Ghana reveal severe pollution levels, likely attributable to ASM activities. This interpretation aligns with the study of Hilson [[41](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR41 "Hilson G. The environmental impact of small-scale gold mining in Ghana: identifying problems and possible solutions. Geogr J. 2002;168:57–72. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/1475-4959.00038
                  
                .")], which highlighted the detrimental effects of ASM on water resources. The CPI values (upstream: 172.62, midstream: 468.68, downstream: 401.31) are significantly above 2.0, denoting severe pollution [[67](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR67 "Zhao X, Gao B, Xu D, Gao L, Yin S. Heavy metal pollution in sediments of the largest reservoir (three gorges reservoir) in China: a review. Environ Sci Pollut Res. 2017;24:20844–58. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s11356-017-9874-8
                  
                .")]. These results underscore the extensive degradation of water quality in the Oda River, consistent with findings from other studies on ASM-impacted water bodies in Ghana [[36](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR36 "Kusi-Ampofo S, Boachie-Yiadom T. Assessing the social and environmental impacts of illegal mining operations in River Bonsa Prepared By Pure Fm-Tarkwa, for the BUSAC Project. Tarkwa, Ghana: 2012.")]. The midstream sampling point exhibits the highest concentrations of pollution, followed by the downstream and upstream locations. This pattern suggests that ASM activities intensify along the river's course, with the most significant impacts observed in the middle reaches. This spatial variation in pollution concentrations is consistent with the typical distribution of ASM operations along river systems in Ghana [[65](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR65 "Mantey J, Nyarko KB, Owusu-Nimo F, Awua KA, Bempah CK, Amankwah RK, et al. Mercury contamination of soil and water media from different illegal artisanal small-scale gold mining operations (galamsey). Heliyon. 2020;6: e04312. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heliyon.2020.e04312
                  
                .")]. Among the analysed parameters, turbidity and Fe concentrations are the most significant contributors to the high CPI values. Elevated turbidity concentrations are characteristic of water bodies affected by ASM, primarily due to increased sedimentation from mining activities [[48](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR48 "Macdonald KF, Lund MA, Blanchette ML, Mccullough CD. Regulation of artisanal small-scale gold mining (ASGM) in Ghana and Indonesia, as currently implemented, fails to adequately protect aquatic ecosystems. Proceedings of International Mine Water Association Symposium, Xuzhou, China: IMWA; 2014, p. 401–5.")]. The elevated concentrations of Fe are likely a result of the mobilisation of Fe from soil and bedrock during mining processes, a common consequence of ASM activities [[68](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR68 "Ato AF, Obiri S, Oscar YD, Frederick AA, Samuel O, David OY, et al. Mining and heavy metal pollution: assessment of aquatic environments in Tarkwa (Ghana) using multivariate statistical analysis. J Environ Statist. 2010;1:1–13.")]. The high Fe concentrations can lead to various health issues if the water is consumed and may also affect aquatic ecosystems negatively [[17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44274-025-00204-y#ref-CR17 "Bansah KJ, Dumakor-Dupey NK, Kansake BA, Assan E, Bekui P. Socioeconomic and environmental assessment of informal artisanal and small-scale mining in Ghana. J Clean Prod. 2018;202:465–75. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/J.JCLEPRO.2018.08.150
                  
                .")]. These findings highlight the urgent need for improved regulation and management of ASM activities in the Oda River basin. ### 3.5 Limitations of the study

The scope of this research was limited to collecting water samples during a single season. Expanding the sampling period to encompass the rainy and dry seasons will be prudent. However, the results reported in this study critically highlight the effects of illegal mining on water bodies in Ghana. The research examined the environmental impacts and public health issues caused by ASM.

## 4 Conclusion

The study results showed a mixed picture: several parameters, such as pH, EC, TDS, and PTE concentrations (except Fe), were within acceptable limits set by the WHO and GSA. However, other parameters such as Fe, TSS, turbidity, faecal coliform, and _E. coli_ concentrations exceeded the safe limits set by WHO and GSA. The CPI values of 172.62, 468.68, and 401.31 in the upstream, midstream, and downstream of the Oda River are above 2.0, suggesting that the freshwater is severely polluted and unfit for human consumption and domestic purposes. Turbidity and Fe were identified as the significant contributors to the pollution of the Oda River.

ASM activities along the Oda Basin have been identified as the main source of pollution of the Oda River. These ASM activities in freshwater bodies hinder the ability of Ghana to achieve SDG 6, particularly indicator 6.1.1 (proportion of the population using safely managed drinking water services). Therefore, the government of Ghana should ban small-scale mining activities in river basins. Local government authorities and traditional leaders should establish an anti-galamsey community task force to tackle illegal mining at the community level. Small-scale mining companies that pollute water bodies should be punished with heavy fines, penalties, and jail time to discourage potential unlawful miners. Effectively enforcing the ban on illicit mining can also help tackle this problem.

## Abstract

Water is an indispensable resource for human health and social well-being. However, the quality of this critical resource is being threatened by both natural and anthropogenic sources. Surface and groundwater resources in the Upper East Region of Ghana are poorly managed and monitored. The water resources in this part of Ghana are contaminated with coliforms, toxic trace metals, and agrochemicals. Most of the parameters for drinking water quality are seriously being violated in various parts of the region. The major sources of surface water and groundwater pollution in the region are the dissolution of minerals, the widespread application of agrochemicals on farms, biological contamination resulting from human and animal fecal matter due to open defecation and mining activities. These have resulted in diverse health-related problems in the region since the contaminated water sources are the only drinking water supplies for rural folks. Fluoride contamination of the groundwater resources is also a major problem in the region, especially in the Bongo District and the Bolgatanga Municipality, which has resulted in cases of dental fluorosis in these parts of the region. There exists no comprehensive review on the water quality in the Upper East Region of Ghana. Therefore, this review is aimed at discussing the quality of the water resources in the region from previously published works in various parts of the region. The review highlights the major pollutants, pollution sources, and the associated health problems. Recommendations have been offered based on the findings to serve as a framework for policy-making in regard to the water resources in the region.

## Abstract

Freshwater resources are continually decreasing in quality and quantity. Approximately, 1% of this freshwater is accessible in lakes, river channels and underground for domestic use. The study reviewed literature on water resources with focus on freshwater, the quality of our freshwater in terms of physical, chemical and biological variables, the main mechanisms of management, and the challenges associated with these mechanisms as well as blending integrated water management with the indigenous or traditional management of water resources for sustainable development and peaceful co-existence. Also the review offered potent recommendations for policy makers to consider sustainable management of freshwater resources. A total of 95 articles were downloaded from Google scholar in water-related issues. The search took place from June to September 2017, and research articles from 1998 to 2018 were reviewed. Basically Ghana is made up of three discharge or outlet systems, namely the Coastal River Systems which is the least and Volta constituting the largest and with the South-Western been the intermediate. Also, freshwater resources usage can be put into two main categories, namely ex situ (withdrawal use) and in situ or in-stream use, and could also be referred to as the consumptive and non-consumptive use, respectively. With the exception of localised pollution engineered by illegal mining and other nuisance perpetuated by indigenes, the quality of water (surface and groundwater) in Ghana is generally better. The review outlined high microbial contamination of water as almost all surface waters are contaminated with either _E. coli_, faecal coliforms or total coliforms or all. However, these contaminations were more prevalent in surface water than groundwater.

In total, the world’s water resources are in excess of about 43,750 km 3 per annum, which disperse widely across the world according to the physical features coupled with patchwork of climates. In the world, USA holds the largest portion of the world’s total freshwater resources estimated to be about 45%; the second largest is Asia with over 28% of freshwater resources, closely followed by Europe with 15.50% and the other continents with 11.50%. Report. ISSN 1020-1203")).

Basically due to growing populations and our constant exploitation of this precious resource to meet, our fundamental needs have jeopardised and corrupted the potential use of freshwater resources. Also climate change as well as fiscal factors coupled with environmental pollution from waste (both municipal and industrial waste), leaching of toxic chemicals from fertilisers and pesticides used in agriculture, has further deepen the woes in the potential use of this freshwater resource for our needs. A direct increase in pollution results in a decrease in the amount of operational water (Nsubuga et al. [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13201-018-0736-4#ref-CR22 "Nsubuga FNW, Namutebi EN, Nsubuga-Ssenfuma M (2014) Water resources of Uganda: an assessment and review. Journal of Water Resource and Protection 6:1297–1315. 
                  https://doi.org/10.4236/jwarp.2014.614120
                  
                
                        ")).

Moreover, rapid increase in population across the globe, notably in the developing countries, presents a significant threat to the water resource as well as been a threat to sustainability prompting the need to carefully handle and protect the resource. The term ‘water management’ broadens over a several sort of activities and disciplines. Water resource management denotes the skilful, efficient as well as effective planning of the limited fresh water resources available for consumption by populace. Water management can be sectioned into three, namely managing water services, then managing the resource and managing the trade-offs needed to equipoise demand and supply (United Nations [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13201-018-0736-4#ref-CR30 "United Nations (UN) (2014) Water resources management. Retrieved June 2016, from 
                  http://www.unwater.org/topics/water-resources-management/en
                  
                
                        ")).

In Ghana, though much has been done on water resources, documentaries, news items and more significantly literature on water resources are more disjointed and not strongly incorporated in policy documents, strategic action plans and reports produced by non-governmental organisations (NGOs), consultants and international entities. The quality of groundwater and surface water resources keeps worsening mainly due to soaring levels of pollution from “galamsey” (illegal mining), waste, leachate from chemical fertilisers and pesticides used in agriculture, chemicals from mining, and use of chemicals in fishing coupled with rapid population growth has entirely left Ghana’s water resources ungovernable. The existing water management strategies employed is not robust enough to cover the challenges. Over the past 6 years and counting, Ghana’s per capita availability of water resources is reducing daily. The effect of climate change leading to variability in precipitation is one of the challenges our country faces at present, which often result in floods as we recorded the June 3 twin disaster in Accra, Ghana in 2014. The review therefore seeks to assess water resources with focus on freshwater, the challenges, the quality of freshwater in terms of chemical, physical and biological variables as well as blending integrated water management with the indigenous or traditional management of water resources for sustainable development and peaceful co-existence.

## The state of water resources in Ghana

Ghana’s water resources are categorised into ground water and surface water; however, there are also impoundments or reservoirs. The sources of surface water resources in Ghana are from three river systems, namely the Coastal river systems, South-Western and Volta (Ghana National Water Policy [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13201-018-0736-4#ref-CR19 "Ministry of Water Resources, Works and Housing, Ghana. (2007). Ghana national water policy")) (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13201-018-0736-4#Fig1)).

### Surface water resources in Ghana

Surface water resources are principally sourced from three river mainstream discharges in Ghana notably: the Coastal River, South-Western and Volta systems. The Red, Black and White Volta Rivers as well as the Oti River comprise of the Volta river systems. The Bia Tano, Ankobra and Pra rivers constitute the South-Western river systems. The Tordzie/Aka, Densu, Ayensu, Ochi-Nakwa and Ochi-Amissah form the Coastal river systems (Ghana National Water Policy [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13201-018-0736-4#ref-CR19 "Ministry of Water Resources, Works and Housing, Ghana. (2007). Ghana national water policy")). These river systems make up 70, 22 and 8%, respectively, of the total land area of about 240,000 km 2. In addition, the sole natural freshwater lake in Ghana is Lake Bosumtwi. This is a meteoritic crater lake located in the forest zone, with a surface area of 50 km 2 and a maximum depth of 78 m (Ghana National Water Policy [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13201-018-0736-4#ref-CR19 "Ministry of Water Resources, Works and Housing, Ghana. (2007). Ghana national water policy"); WRC Ghana [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13201-018-0736-4#ref-CR33 "Water Resource Commission Ghana (2012) National integrated water resources management (IWRM) plan. Water Resources Commission Ministry of Water Resources Works and Housing")).

### Groundwater resources in Ghana

Ghana’s groundwater resources are made up of three geological formations with 54, 45 and 1% for the basement complex (metamorphic rocks and crystalline igneous), the consolidated sedimentary formations, and the Cenozoic and Mesozoic sedimentary rocks, respectively (Ghana National Water Policy [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13201-018-0736-4#ref-CR19 "Ministry of Water Resources, Works and Housing, Ghana. (2007). Ghana national water policy")). Occurrence of groundwater in the basement complex is linked to the development of secondary porosity hence causing the fracturing, jointing, shearing and weathering. Aquifers depth normally ranged from 10 to 60 m with yields hardly exceeding 6 metres cubic per hour (Ghana National Water Policy [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13201-018-0736-4#ref-CR19 "Ministry of Water Resources, Works and Housing, Ghana. (2007). Ghana national water policy"); WRC Ghana [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13201-018-0736-4#ref-CR33 "Water Resource Commission Ghana (2012) National integrated water resources management (IWRM) plan. Water Resources Commission Ministry of Water Resources Works and Housing")). The Cenozoic and Mesozoic formations that usually occur in the extreme South Eastern and Western part of Ghana are also limestone aquifers with depth range of 120 to 300 m. The limestone aquifers have an average yield of about 184 cubic metres per hour (Ghana National Water Policy [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13201-018-0736-4#ref-CR19 "Ministry of Water Resources, Works and Housing, Ghana. (2007). Ghana national water policy"); WRC Ghana [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13201-018-0736-4#ref-CR35 "Water Resources Commission (2007) Annual Report. WRC, Accra")).
