 ![Image 2: Section image](https://custom-images.strikinglycdn.com/res/hrscywv4p/image/upload/c_limit,fl_lossy,h_9000,w_1200,f_auto,q_auto/10524970/1258_692439.jpeg)        

    

Andrea Farnham is an epidemiologist and academic researcher specializing in using digital data to track population movement and health.

**Expertise and Interests**

    *   Global mobility and health
    *   mHealth studies
    *   Health impact assessment
    *   Statistics and R Software
    *   Geospatial analyses in Google Earth Engine and QGIS

Affiliations

    *   Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute, University of Basel
    *   Epidemiology, Biostatistics, and Prevention Institute, University of Zurich

*     ## Current Projects     #### A selection of current projects.       ![Image 3: Section image](https://custom-images.strikinglycdn.com/res/hrscywv4p/image/upload/c_limit,fl_lossy,h_9000,w_1200,f_auto,q_auto/10524970/782287_686876.jpeg)        ### MIGRANT(h) Project    In northern Mozambique, a volatile combination of natural disasters, violence and conflict, and COVID-19 have all combined to create a humanitarian crisis where it is estimated that over half a million people have already been displaced,  
many of them women, children or other vulnerable groups. In this project, we propose to innovate disaster response by using readily available digital data and tools (i.e. satellite data, machine learning techniques) and HIA methods (e.g. semi-quantitative risk assessment, quantitative calculation of health status of migratory populations at baseline) to estimate and geo-locate the population displacements and environmental changes (e.g. destruction of infrastructure, flooding) caused by the crisis and identify the likely short and long-term health effects of these population displacements.           ![Image 4: Section image](https://custom-images.strikinglycdn.com/res/hrscywv4p/image/upload/c_limit,fl_lossy,h_9000,w_1200,f_auto,q_auto/10524970/986177_955566.png)        ### HIA4SD Project    The HIA4SD project (full title: ‘Health impact assessment for engaging natural resource extraction projects in sustainable development in producer regions’) is an inter- and transdisciplinary research initiative implemented in four African countries (Burkina Faso, Ghana, Mozambique and Tanzania). The overarching objective of the HIA4SD project is to conduct research – complemented by a strong capacity building component – that will inform and facilitate a policy dialogue for strengthening the application of impact assessment as a regulatory mechanism (i) to avoid negative effects of natural resource extraction projects (NREPs) on public health; and (ii) to actively engage NREPs – and any other large infrastructure developments – in the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and, thus, development in Africa.

See: [Home - HIA4SD](link_1)           ![Image 5: Section image](https://custom-images.strikinglycdn.com/res/hrscywv4p/image/upload/c_limit,fl_lossy,h_9000,w_1200,f_auto,q_auto/10524970/700907_540077.jpeg)        ### TOURIST Studies    Travel medicine research often relies on surveys administered to individuals long before or after their travel, meaning that evidence-based medical advice during travel is scarce and subject to recall bias. New technology means that every traveler could have an e-doctor in their pocket. I developed a smartphone application (TOURIST) together with computer scientists that conducted groundbreaking research in travel medicine by tracking traveler health and behavior in almost real-time and tagging it to precise locations during their trips. It was the first study of its kind in travel medicine. After the success of the original study, a second, much larger follow-up study was conducted. While the initial studies have established the acceptability and rigor of the platform as a data collection tool, I believe it is only the first step a paradigm shift towards digitizing travel medicine.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/)Abstract

### Background

The African continent hosts many industrial mining projects, and many more are planned due to recent prospecting discoveries and increasing demand for various minerals to promote a low-carbon future. The extraction of natural resources in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) represents an opportunity for economic development but also poses a threat to population health through rapid urbanisation and environmental degradation. Children could benefit from improved economic growth through various channels such as access to high-quality food, better sanitation, and clean water. However, mining can increase food insecurity and trigger local competition over safe drinking water. Child health can be threatened by exposure to mining-related air, noise, and water pollution. To assess the impact of mines on child health, we analyse socio-demographic, health, and mining data before and after several mining projects were commissioned in SSA.

### Results

Data of 90,951 children living around 81 mining sites in 23 countries in SSA were analysed for child mortality indicators, and 79,962 children from 59 mining areas in 18 SSA countries were analysed for diarrhoea, cough, and anthropometric indicators. No effects of the launch of new mining projects on overall under-five mortality were found (adjusted Odds Ratio (aOR): 0.88; 95% Confidence Interval (CI): 0.68–1.14). However, activation of mining projects reduced the mortality risk among neonates (0–30 days) by 45% (aOR: 0.55; 95% CI: 0.37–0.83) and risk for a child to develop diarrhoeal diseases by 32% (aOR: 0.68; 95% CI: 0,51–0.90). The timing analysis of observed changes showed that there is a significant decline in the risk for childhood diarrhoea (aOR: 0.69; 95% CI: 0.49–0.97), and the mean height-for-age z-scores by 28 percentage points, during the prospection and construction phase; i.e., within four years to the initiation of extraction activity. No effects were found for cough and weight-for-height.

### Conclusion

The results presented suggest that the impacts of mining on child health vary throughout the mine’s life cycle. Mining development likely contributes positively to the income and livelihoods of the impacted communities in the initial years of mining operations, particularly the prospection and construction phase; these potential benefits are likely to be at least partially offset by food insecurity and environmental pollution during early and later mining stages, respectively. Further research is warranted to better understand these health impacts and to identify policies that can help sustain the positive initial health impacts of mining projects in the long term.

### Supplementary Information

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12992-022-00797-6.

**Keywords:**Child morbidity, Child mortality, Demographic and health survey, Diarrhoea, Mining, Nutrition, Sub-Saharan Africa

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/)Introduction

The African continent holds one-third of global natural resources [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR1), [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR2)] and hosts more than 2000 industrial mining projects at different development stages [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR2), [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR3)]. This number might further increase with the growing demand for various minerals to promote a low-carbon future [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR1)]. While the extraction of natural resources represents an opportunity for countries rich in natural resources in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), the impact of large-scale mining projects on the health of young children remains unclear.

On the one hand, mining projects can positively influence determinants of health and, thus, improve child health. For example, the development of mining projects has the potential to increase the share of workers with regular incomes – including women of reproductive age [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR4), [5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR5)] – and, thus, improves households’ capacity to buy healthier foods, access health care, and send the children to school [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR5)–[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR7)]. Furthermore, mining projects can improve housing conditions, including proper sanitation and safe water [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR8), [9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR9)]. In turn, better housing, sanitation, and water conditions can reduce the incidence of environment-related diseases such as respiratory infections, diarrhoeal diseases, malaria, and undernutrition [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR10)–[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR12)].

On the other hand, it has been reported that mining activities can have adverse effects on child health and development [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR13), [14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR14)]. For example, mining activities can negatively affect local and regional agricultural production through environmental degradation and changes in land use [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR15), [16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR16)]. Consequently, food insecurity can increase, which is of particular concern for young children and pregnant women [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR6), [17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR17), [18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR18)]. Additionally, mining projects have high energy and water demand, potentially triggering local competition over existing resources, including access to safe drinking water [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR19)–[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR21)]. In the contexts where natural resources are extracted, adverse environmental impacts such as air, noise, and water pollution are a significant concern for child health [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR20), [22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR22), [23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR23)]. Studies found that exposure to environmentally poor conditions during the early stages of human life, including in-utero exposure, can result in long-term adverse effects on cognitive abilities, respiratory functions, and nutritional status [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR14), [17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR17), [24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR24)].

Estimated impacts of mining projects on child health outcomes, such as diarrhoea, respiratory infections, and child mortality, have been highly heterogeneous to date [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR6), [25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR25), [26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR26)]. One reason for the high heterogeneity seen in the empirical literature is the often differential focus on early (opening phase) vs. late (extraction phase) of mining [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR27), [28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR28)]. It also seems plausible that the heterogeneity of the currently available results is due to the narrow focus of current studies either on just one country or one mineral (such as gold) or both [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR6), [7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR7), [14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR14), [29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8802519/#CR29)].
